cards.title: Reading: AWS Automated Reasoning checks
cards.md: The concepts page ("Findings and validation results" and "Validation results reference", read 2026-10-23) lists seven results: VALID, INVALID, SATISFIABLE, IMPOSSIBLE, TRANSLATION_AMBIGUOUS, TOO_COMPLEX and NO_TRANSLATIONS. cards.title: Lean's vcgen, after your own generator
cards.md: Lean's experimental `vcgen` tactic generates verification conditions for a program and its specification. The course runs it on a Mini-Plinth-style command beside your own checker, after you have built yours. It proves the guarded Transfer once it is given a weakest-precondition instance and one specification per construct, and with the guard weakened it leaves an unproved goal: the same obligation your checker answers with a satisfiable negation. {{run:RUN-lean-vcgen}} {{run:RUN-vcgen-cmd}} Lean's reference calls `vcgen` experimental and subject to change (read 2026-10-23). Pins: {{run:RUN-twin-pins}}.

cards.title: Cedar's symbolic compiler
cards.md: Cedar, an authorization language, compiles its policies to SMT and proves that compilation sound and complete in Lean (arXiv 2407.01688, 2024). Those are the two halves of what a verification-condition generator owes you. With the invariant encoded exactly, it is sound when its step relation contains every real step, and complete when it contains nothing else. Replaying a satisfiable model in the interpreter tests completeness, and known-false fixtures with a premise witness test soundness. SymCert (FMCAD 2026) put production SMT analyses through Lean proofs, and those proofs caught encoder bugs. Pins: {{run:RUN-twin-pins}}.

cards.title: TigerBeetle's pending balances
cards.md: TigerBeetle's flag `debits_must_not_exceed_credits` rejects a transfer when the pending debits, the posted debits and the new amount together exceed the posted credits. Its two-phase transfers reserve the pending amount, so a later post or void never breaks the balance invariant (documentation read 2026-10-23). It is the production shape of the Hold guard in S4.L6: the guard counts what is already held. Pins: {{run:RUN-twin-pins}}.

cards.title: A solver that was wrong
cards.md: Z3 issue 11179, reported 2026-10-15, shows a solver answering `unsat` on inputs that are satisfiable, in nonlinear real exponentiation. The answer depends on the solver's version and on how the query enters it. The recorded run replays it. {{run:RUN-z3-11179}} The defect sits outside the fragment your checker handles. What carries over is that an `unsat` names its solver, its version and its entry path, and stays uncertified until something independent checks it.

interface.vcgen_docstring_opening:
`vcgen` will break down a Hoare triple proof goal like `⦃P⦄ prog ⦃Q⦄` into verification conditions,
provided that all functions used in `prog` have specifications registered with `@[spec]`.

`vcgen` is experimental and subject to change. `set_option experimental.vcgen true` acknowledges
its experimental status and silences the warning that each call reports.

### Program types

`vcgen` works on any program type `Prog` that carries a `Std.WP.WP` interpretation. A monad
is one such program type. An inductive type of commands is another, once its weakest precondition is
defined in terms of an operational semantics.

experimental.vcgen.descr: acknowledge that the `vcgen` tactic is experimental and subject to change; `true` silences the warning that each `vcgen` call reports

experimental.intrinsic.descr: acknowledge that the intrinsic verification syntax (the contract clauses of a `def`, the `assert` element, and the `invariant` and `decreasing` clauses of a loop) is experimental and subject to change; `true` silences the warning that each of these forms reports

The `ensures` clause is part of the experimental intrinsic verification syntax; `set_option experimental.intrinsic true` acknowledges its experimental status and silences this warning.

The course pins the version 18 pages rather than the current ones, because the current pages move when the next major version is released.

cards.title: Optional reading
cards.md: Hermitage (Kleppmann, CC BY 4.0, https://github.com/ept/hermitage): the README summary table and the sections of its PostgreSQL page on lost update, read skew and write skew. Ports and Grittner, "Serializable Snapshot Isolation in PostgreSQL", PVLDB 5(12), 2012. Kingsbury and Alvaro, "Elle", PVLDB 14(3), 2020. All read 2026-10-23.

cards.title: PostgreSQL's own isolation specs
cards.md: PostgreSQL tests its isolation levels with isolationtester specs, the format this stage's catalog copies: each spec declares sessions and steps, and a recorded output file says what the server did. One spec re-checks a WHERE clause after a concurrent update; another lists no permutations, so every interleaving runs. Pins are in {{run:RUN-twin-pins}}. Which interleavings commit both transactions, and why are they exactly the serial orders?

cards.title: Cedar's differential random testing
cards.md: Cedar compares its production implementation with its formal model on randomly generated inputs (https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.01688, section 4, read 2026-10-23; pins in {{run:RUN-twin-pins}}). Section 4.3 notes that full line coverage still sent many inputs only through error handling.

cards.title: Hermitage
cards.md: Hermitage runs one set of isolation tests against many databases (https://github.com/ept/hermitage, read 2026-10-23). Its PostgreSQL results come from an old release. The course re-records them on the version it pins and names every history by its compilation pattern, never by isolation level alone.

cards.title: TigerBeetle's transfer results
cards.md: TigerBeetle's `create_transfers` names every refusal as a result code, from `accounts_must_be_different` to `overflows_credits_posted` (https://docs.tigerbeetle.com/reference/requests/create_transfers/, read 2026-10-23; pins in {{run:RUN-twin-pins}}). Map your typed outcomes onto its results.

cards.title: Jepsen on PostgreSQL, 2020-06-12
cards.md: Jepsen reported G2-item anomalies under SERIALIZABLE in several PostgreSQL releases, including 12.3, caused by a conflict-detection bug that was fixed in 2020 (https://jepsen.io/analyses/postgresql-12.3, section 3.2, read 2026-10-23). S6.L9 asks what your claim assumes about the database underneath it, and this report is the dated example.

authored.defence: Untimed, over at least two sessions within a week of the lab. Part A is twelve unseen probes with a call on each, including what differential tests establish and what they cannot, and the four SQL mismatches: NULL, bags, numeric overflow and serialization failures. Part B is four mutations of your own compiler and runtime, predicted first: read-modify-write compilation, a dropped rowcount check, a retry policy that handles one failure code only, and a pool set to READ COMMITTED. Part C is four audit cases, at least one of them sound. Part D is a short explanation of R(S, D) and of what one simulation step checks.

authored.summary: Give your system users, teams, roles, documents and sharing, and state the read rule the roadmap gives you: a user may see a document when they are a team member or it is explicitly shared. You write that rule as Datalog, check it with Z3, and enforce it with row-level security in PostgreSQL. Then you meet what enforcement leaves open. A check on every read is not noninterference, so you say who the observer is, which worlds it must not tell apart, what your system releases on purpose, and why revoking access cannot unsee what was already delivered.

cards.title: Cedar's three layers of evidence
cards.md: Cedar, an authorization language, backs its authorizer with three layers: a Lean model with properties checked in Lean, such as default deny and "forbid trumps permit"; a per-change symbolic analysis that returns a distinguishing request; and daily differential random testing of the Rust authorizer against the model. S7.L2, S7.L3 and S7.L4 each take one layer. See the [Cedar paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.04651) and [How We Built Cedar](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.01688). Pins: {{run:RUN-twin-pins}}.

cards.title: Zanzibar's new enemy
cards.md: Zanzibar, Google's authorization system, names a case that a permission check alone misses: a person is removed from a document's ACL, new content is added, and a check against a stale copy of the ACL still lets them read it. Section 2.2 of the [Zanzibar paper](https://www.usenix.org/conference/atc19/presentation/pang) states it, and S7.L8 reproduces it on a model whose ACL replica lags. The paper (read 2026-10-23) describes a closed system, so there is no commit to pin.

cards.title: TigerBeetle: reliable transaction submission
cards.md: TigerBeetle's page "Reliable Transaction Submission" (read 2026-10-23) has the client generate the id, persist it "before submitting the transfer", and resend with the same id; a duplicate returns `exists`. Set your table of crash windows beside it, and ask which windows persisting first closes. Pins: {{run:RUN-twin-pins}}. See [docs.tigerbeetle.com](https://docs.tigerbeetle.com/).

cards.title: CCF: smart casual verification
cards.md: CCF checks its implementation against its TLA+ specification, with trace validation run in CI, and reports six consensus bugs (Howard et al., NSDI 2025; [arXiv 2406.17455](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.17455), v2, 2024-10-16). Read where its trace module aligns a coarser grain of atomicity, and how CI decides a trace failed. Pins: {{run:RUN-twin-pins}}.

cards.title: TigerBeetle: the VOPR
cards.md: TigerBeetle's simulator runs a cluster "running real code" against "network, storage and process faults" from a seed (the Safety page, read 2026-10-23). Compare it with your own harness: where a seed fixes the fault schedule, how a failing seed replays, and where invariants are checked. Pins: {{run:RUN-twin-pins}}.

cards.title: Stripe: documented key pruning
cards.md: Stripe's API reference, "Idempotent requests" (read 2026-10-21, re-read 2026-10-23), says that for API v1 a key can be removed once it is at least 24 hours old, and that a key reused after the original is pruned makes a new request ([the page](https://docs.stripe.com/api/idempotent_requests)). The outage that outlives that retention is specimen SP-8.5: {{run:RUN-tlc-key-ttl}}.

authored.summary: Translate a small subset of Mini-Plinth into a simpler intermediate representation, prove that the translation preserves what a client can observe, break the proof with a bad optimization, validate generated SQL one command at a time, and keep three claims apart: the command preserves invariants, the compiler preserves meaning, and the runtime follows the target. cards.title: CompCert
cards.md: CompCert states its preservation theorem as a backward simulation and lists the parts of the compiler its proof does not cover (manual, chapter 1; `common/Smallstep.v`; Leroy, CACM 2009). Your theorem has the same shape and the same kind of list. Pinned in {{run:RUN-twin-pins}}.

cards.title: Alive2
cards.md: Alive2 is bounded translation validation for LLVM. It checks each optimization's output within a bound and reports a counterexample when it finds one (Lopes et al., PLDI 2021). S9.L2 and LAB-9.1 are the same move on your compiler. Pinned in {{run:RUN-twin-pins}}.

cards.title: Isabelle HOL-IMP

authored.defence: Two mini-Defences, each sampling only its own half, untimed and taken over at least two sessions within a week. The first follows the observations lesson and covers the stack machine, validator witnesses, the IR and observers that miss aborts. Its mutations of your own work include dropping `generalizing stk`, closing an IR golden with `native_decide`, reading both balances first and evaluating the amount twice. The second follows the last lab stage and covers the case lemmas, bad optimizations, SQL instances, step and size observers and the trusted base. Its mutations include making aborts unobservable, hoisting the debit, validating shape only and weakening R. Each ends with an explain-back: the refinement relation and the IR's boundary in the first, the three claims and why they stay apart in the second.

authored.summary: Assemble the Core. You wire the parser, typechecker and interpreter of Stage 3, the checker of Stage 4, the compiler and runtime of Stage 6 and the simulator of Stage 8 into one pipeline that you own, and you re-run each part's own gate before it goes in. Then the Core judges an agent's proposal in front of you: you choose the checker for each part of its claim, refute it with a witness that replays or prove a stated fragment, keep a sound command and strengthen a weak invariant, or fail closed, and you run the corrected command on PostgreSQL under your runtime and record the demonstration end to end. You finish by exporting a report from your claim graph and publishing a bundle that says exactly what each line establishes, what it assumes and what it does not cover. The course plans about six weeks for all of this, shown as ranges.

cards.title: Reading, minimum path
cards.md: Read 2026-10-23. About half an hour to an hour. Bloomfield, Netkachova and Rushby, "Defeaters and Eliminative Argumentation in Assurance 2.0" (SRI-CSL-2024-01, https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.15800), section 6, "Defeaters and Confidence". Goodenough, Weinstock and Klein, "Eliminative Argumentation: A Basis for Arguing Confidence in System Properties" (CMU/SEI-2015-TR-005, 2015-02-25), section 2.1 for m|n, section 2.2 for the three kinds of doubt, section 3.1, "Unidentified Defeaters", and section 3.5, "True Defeaters (Counterevidence)". The Lean Language Reference for the pinned Lean release, "Validating a Lean Proof": its opening threat model, "Gold Standard: comparator and external checkers" and "Remaining Issues". The CompCert manual, chapter 1, sections 1.2 and 1.3: what its proof covers, what it does not, and "observable behavior".

cards.title: Reading, optional
cards.md: Read 2026-10-23. Gohar, Hunter, Cohen and Lutz, "A Taxonomy of Real-World Defeaters in Safety Assurance Cases" (https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.00238), sections IV-A to IV-G: the checklist for hunting doubts. The Lean community's page "Did you prove it?": "Does the repository compile? Is the proof being checked?" and "Does your work prove what you claim it proves?". The PostgreSQL manual, section 13.2.3, "Serializable Isolation Level" (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/transaction-iso.html): the retry requirement, and a guarantee stated for committed SERIALIZABLE transactions.

cards.title: Production twin: Cedar's release gate
cards.md: Cedar ships a release only when its evidence is up to date: "A new version of Cedar isn't released unless its model, proofs, and differential tests are up to date" (Hietala and Torlak, "Lean Into Verified Software Development", AWS Open Source Blog, 2024-04-08, section "How Cedar uses Lean for verification-guided development"). That is the shape of this stage: a report that says which evidence stands behind each line, and a check that fails when the evidence is out of date. Pins are in {{run:RUN-twin-pins}}.

cards.title: Dated incident: OEIS Open, 2026-08-12
cards.md: A headline of 147 results out of 492 became 144 out of 492 under comparator's verdicts (Adamczewski, "OEIS Open", https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11941, section 2.3, "Proof verification", read 2026-10-23). The difference is why your report shows which checker re-checked each line, and why a discrepancy is a doubt and never a footnote.

authored.defence: Untimed, over at least two sessions within a week of publishing the bundle, with your agent closed. Part A is twelve unseen probes across all seven outcome families, with one item each on the two ideas Stage 8 marked as thresholds, that committing is not sending and that at-least-once delivery duplicates, and four probes on this stage: a fresh agent proposal to triage, a report line to stamp, what your report establishes, and a doubt status. Part B is seven seeded mutations of your own Core, one for each component you own, which you predict first and the component's own checker then grades: the parser, the typechecker, the checker, the interpreter, the compiler, the runtime and the simulator. Part C is four cases, one from your own repo, harvested from your agent's commits or generated when none touched a statement, and three from the cross-stage pool, at least one of them sound. Part D asks you to explain, in two minutes, what the report establishes and what it does not, and then to compare a three-idea self-check with Part A. It is required and uncredited.
